The same idempotency key on every attempt, so the provider refunds only once
A new payment id for each attempt, so the provider does not reject duplicates
explain: A timeout only tells you that you stopped waiting: the provider may have processed the first refund. Sending the same idempotency key on every attempt lets it recognise the retry and answer with the first result (M02). A new id per attempt is precisely how a customer gets refunded twice.

q: This integration test against PostgreSQL fails with '4500499' !== 4999. What is the cause?
options: sum() is a bigint, which node-postgres returns as a string, so + concatenates
The cart has a second line priced 499 cents that the test fixture forgot to remove
TypeScript compiled + as string concatenation because of the generic type on query
PostgreSQL returned the sum in euros, not in cents
explain: On PostgreSQL 18.6, pg_typeof of the sum is bigint, and the pg-types README states that node-postgres returns int8 results as strings. '4500' + 499 is '4500499'. TypeScript emits no code for +: the generic on query is an unchecked assertion, so the type said number while the value was a string.

q: A test of the export "orders sorted by total" fails. What does this line print?
explain: Without a comparator, sort converts the values to strings and compares them in UTF-16 order, so "999" comes after "4500" (verified on Node 24). Pass a comparator: toSorted((a, b) => a - b) printed [ 999, 1200, 4500 ] and leaves the original array untouched.

q: paymentStatus() takes about 300 ms and deliveryEta() about 600 ms; neither needs the other's result. How long does this handler take, and what is the fix?
options: About 600 ms already, because Node starts the awaits in parallel by default
About 900 ms; with Promise.all over the two calls it drops to about 600 ms
About 900 ms, and nothing can be done without worker threads
About 300 ms, because the second await starts while the first one is still pending
explain: Each await waits before the next call starts, so the times add up: measured on Node 24 with timers, 911 ms sequentially and 604 ms with Promise.all, which starts both calls and waits for the slower. Waiting on I/O needs no worker thread.

q: In the bug bash, only GET /orders/:id is slow. The trace shows 850 ms in one SQL span; other routes and the event loop metrics are normal. What do you do next?
options: Add replicas of the API
Take a CPU profile of the Node process
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on that query and read its plan
Add a cache in front of the route before investigating further
explain: The measurement already points at one query, so the next step is its plan, which shows a sequential scan or a bad join (M08). A CPU profile is the tool when every route is slow and the event loop is busy (M01), which is not the case; a cache or replicas hide the cause without finding it.

q: The CEO asks you in one sentence: "Make checkout faster." What do you do before writing any code?
options: Start optimising the slowest SQL query you already know of in the checkout
Add a cache in front of the checkout so that the CEO sees quick results
Ask what "faster" means, measure the baseline, and agree on a target
Plan a rewrite of the checkout in a faster framework such as Fastify
explain: "Faster" can mean server latency, page load, fewer steps or higher conversion, and each leads to different work. Clarifying the goal, measuring the baseline and agreeing on success is what the question is designed to hear. Starting with the query you already know solves a problem nobody has confirmed.

q: In an ES module, what does this function print when called?
options: 5000, then EUR, because both declarations are hoisted with their values
undefined, then a ReferenceError
A ReferenceError on the first line, before anything prints
undefined, then undefined, since both are hoisted
explain: The var is hoisted and initialized to undefined, so the first log prints undefined. The const is hoisted but uninitialized: reading it in its temporal dead zone throws "Cannot access 'currency' before initialization" (measured on Node 24). Two undefined values would be the behaviour if both were var.

q: A function created inside another function reads one of its variables. What does the inner function keep?
options: A copy of the variable's value at the moment the function was created
Nothing: the variable is freed when the outer function returns
Access to the variable itself, so it sees later changes
A copy that is refreshed only when the outer function is called again
explain: A closure keeps the variable binding, not a snapshot, and keeps it alive as long as the inner function is reachable. That is why listeners created in a var loop all read the final index. The "copy at creation" idea is the misconception the loop question tests.

q: In an ES module, [1250, 399].map(priceFormatter.format) throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'locale')", while priceFormatter.format(1250) works. Why?
options: map calls it as a plain function, so this is undefined in strict code
map calls it with this set to the array, which has no locale property
Intl.NumberFormat cannot be created inside an array callback
Methods written with the shorthand syntax lose their body when passed as values
explain: Passing priceFormatter.format hands over the function without its object, and map calls it as a plain function; ES modules are strict, so this is undefined (measured). map only uses its optional second argument as this, and none was given, so the array is not this.

q: Which statement about arrow functions and this is true?
options: call and bind set its this, exactly as they do for regular functions
Its this is always the global object, even inside a method
Its this is the object it is stored on, like a method shorthand
It takes this from the surrounding code; call and bind cannot change it
explain: Arrows have no this of their own: they read the this of the scope where they are written. Measured: calling an arrow class field with .call({ count: 99 }) still used the instance's count. Storing an arrow on an object does not make the object its this.

q: For const cart = new Cart(), where does the addLine method defined in the class body live?
options: On cart itself, copied there by the constructor on every new
On Cart.prototype, shared by every instance through the prototype chain
On the Cart function itself, as a static property shared by instances
In a hidden per-instance method table created by the engine
explain: Class methods are installed once on Cart.prototype; each instance links to it. Measured: Object.hasOwn(cart, 'addLine') is false and Object.hasOwn(Cart.prototype, 'addLine') is true. Only fields, such as #lines or an arrow function field, are created on each instance.

q: A TypeScript class declares private lines; another declares #lines. What differs at run time?
options: Nothing: both are erased by the compiler and become ordinary properties
Both are enforced at run time, but #lines is faster because it skips the prototype
private is erased at compile time; #lines is unreachable from outside the class
private hides the property from JSON.stringify and Object.keys; #lines does not
explain: TypeScript's private is a compile-time check only, so bracket access or plain JavaScript still reach the property. A # field is private for the engine: measured, it does not appear in Object.keys or JSON.stringify, and cart['#lines'] is undefined.

q: A quantity input is cleared, so its value is ''. What is '' == 0, and why?
options: false, because a string never equals a number without a cast
true, because == converts the empty string to the number 0
false, because the empty string converts to NaN, and NaN equals nothing
It throws a TypeError, because == refuses to compare different types
explain: When == compares a string with a number, it converts the string to a number, and Number('') is 0 (measured). That is how removeEmptyLines dropped the line. NaN is what you get from Number('abc'), not from the empty string.

q: Why can a bundler remove an unused export of an ES module but not of a CommonJS module?
options: ES modules are always smaller after minification, so unused code stands out
CommonJS modules are evaluated twice, once per bundle, so code cannot be dropped
Only ES modules can run in a browser, so CommonJS code is never bundled
Static import and export reveal the graph before running; require() is a run-time call
explain: Static declarations let the bundler see which exports are imported without executing anything; measured with Vite 8.3.4, an unused export disappeared from the bundle. require() can take a computed path and run anywhere, so the bundler cannot know what is used.

q: What makes an object usable in for...of and with spread?
options: A Symbol.iterator method returning an object with next()
A length property and numeric keys, like an array
Being created by a class, whose instances are iterable by default
A forEach method, which for...of calls for each value
explain: That is the iteration protocol: an iterable returns an iterator, whose next() gives { value, done }. A plain object with length and numeric keys is array-like, not iterable, and for...of on a plain object throws "is not iterable" (measured).

q: You call structuredClone(new Money(1250)), where Money is a class with a #cents field and a format() method. What do you get?
options: A Money instance with the same #cents and the same methods
A DataCloneError, because class instances cannot be cloned
A plain object with the public fields only: no methods, no #cents
A Money instance whose #cents is reset to undefined
explain: The structured clone algorithm copies plain data and does not walk the prototype chain or duplicate private elements; measured in Node 24 and Chromium, the copy was { currency: 'EUR' } and instanceof Money was false. DataCloneError is thrown for functions, not for class instances.

q: What distinguishes a WeakMap from a Map?
options: Its keys do not keep their objects alive; it is not iterable and has no size
It frees its entries after a fixed delay, like a cache with a time limit
It accepts any key type, including strings, but holds its values weakly
It is faster than Map, so it suits large caches keyed by product id
explain: A WeakMap entry disappears when its key object is no longer reachable elsewhere; keys must be objects or unregistered symbols, and a string key throws (measured). A cache keyed by string ids therefore cannot be a WeakMap: it needs a bounded Map such as an LRU.

q: What happens when this code runs?
options: It prints 10, from the outer variable
It prints undefined, as a var would
It prints 20, the hoisted value
It throws a ReferenceError
explain: The inner let total shadows the outer one for the whole function body, and the log reads it in its temporal dead zone: "Cannot access 'total' before initialization" (measured on Node 24). Printing 10 would need the outer variable to be visible, but the inner declaration hides it from the start of the block.

q: What does this print?
options: [undefined, undefined, undefined]
explain: The per-iteration binding only applies to a let declared in the for header. Here i is declared once outside the loop, so every arrow closes over the same variable, which is 3 when they run (measured). Writing let inside the header would print [0, 1, 2].

q: What does this print?
options: cart-1 cart-2 cart-3
cart-1 cart-1 cart-1
cart-1 cart-2 cart-1
cart-2 cart-3 cart-2
explain: Each call to createIdGenerator creates a new scope with its own next, and each returned arrow keeps its own. next++ returns the old value, so the first call gives cart-1 (measured). A shared counter, the cart-3 option, would need next to live outside the factory.

q: In an ES module, what happens when cart.labels() is called?
options: It throws a TypeError: the inner function's this is undefined
It returns ['1250 EUR', '399 EUR']: the inner function inherits this
It returns ['1250 undefined', '399 undefined'] from the global object
It throws a ReferenceError: currency is not defined in that scope
explain: labels is called as a method, so its own this is cart, but the inner function is called by map as a plain function and gets its own this: undefined in strict code, so this.currency throws (measured). An arrow callback would read the method's this and return the EUR labels. The undefined labels appear only in old non-module scripts, where this is the global object.

q: What does the last line print?
options: admin
back office
undefined
storefront
explain: bind returns a function whose this is fixed for good: binding it again or calling it with call cannot change it, so the first bind wins (measured: storefront). The back office option assumes the last bind overrides, which is the usual misconception.

q: Given the Cart class with a #lines field and static isCart(value) that returns #lines in value, what does this print?
code:
const fake = Object.create(Cart.prototype);
console.log(fake instanceof Cart, Cart.isCart(fake));
options: false false
true false
true true
It throws a TypeError, because fake has no #lines
explain: instanceof only checks whether Cart.prototype is in the chain, and Object.create put it there, so it is true. No constructor ran, so the object has no #lines, and the #lines in check returns false without throwing (measured). That is why a brand check is more reliable than instanceof.

q: What does this print?
options: Product Mug
It throws, because label was replaced after mug was created
New Mug
undefined
explain: mug does not copy the methods: it links to Product.prototype and looks label up there at call time, so it sees the replacement (measured: New Mug). Product Mug would require the instance to hold its own copy of the method.

q: What does this print?
explain: + is evaluated left to right: 1 + 2 is 3, then 3 + '3' concatenates to '33'; '1' + 2 starts a string, so the result is '123'; - always converts to numbers, so '5' - 2 is 3 (measured). The '15' option assumes 2 + 3 is computed first.

q: A product card shows line.quantity || 1 as the default quantity. A customer sets the quantity to 0 to keep the line but not buy it, and the card shows 1. Which fix would you ship?
options: line.quantity ?? 1, which falls back only for null and undefined
Number(line.quantity) || 1, so that string quantities are converted
line.quantity == 0 ? 1 : line.quantity, to handle zero explicitly
Math.max(line.quantity, 1), so the quantity is never below 1
explain: || falls back for every falsy value, and 0 is falsy, so 0 || 1 is 1; ?? falls back only for null and undefined, so 0 ?? 1 is 0 (measured). Converting with Number keeps the || problem, and the == 0 version forces the same wrong default on purpose.

q: cart-store exports let itemCount = 0 and function addItem() { itemCount += 1; }. What do the two importers print?
options: 1 and 1
0 and 0
0 and 1
1 and 0
explain: An ES import is a live binding to the exporter's variable, so it reads the incremented value. CommonJS destructuring copies the value present in module.exports at require time, and addItem changes only the module's local variable (measured on Node 24: 1, then 0).

q: What does this print?
options: start, created, address
created, start, address
created, address
start, after address, created, address
explain: Calling a generator function runs none of its body; it returns a paused generator. The first next() runs up to the first yield, printing start, then returns address (measured). The body never reaches after address because next() is not called again.

q: What does this print?
options: It throws, because a generator cannot be spread twice
explain: A generator object is an iterator, and an iterator can be consumed once: the second spread finds it done and produces an empty array (measured). Calling promoCodes() again, or making a class iterable with a generator method, gives a fresh iterator each time.

q: The Undo snapshot is made with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(cart)). What do typeof snapshot.updatedAt and snapshot.lines give, if updatedAt is a Date and lines a Map with one entry?
options: 'object' (a Date) and an equal Map
'string' and an equal Map
'object' and an empty object
'string' and an empty object
explain: JSON.stringify calls Date's toJSON, so the date comes back as an ISO string, and a Map has no enumerable own properties, so it becomes {} (measured). structuredClone would keep both the Date and the Map, which is why it fits an in-memory snapshot.

q: The cart drawer sorts prices in cents with prices.sort(), where prices is [1250, 399, 10000, 900]. What is the result, and what else happens?
options: [399, 900, 1250, 10000], and prices is unchanged
[399, 900, 1250, 10000], and prices is sorted in place
[10000, 1250, 399, 900], and prices is sorted in place
[10000, 1250, 399, 900], and prices is unchanged
explain: Without a comparator, sort converts values to strings and compares them, so '10000' comes before '1250' (measured), and sort mutates the array it is called on. prices.toSorted((a, b) => a - b) returns a new, numerically sorted array and leaves prices alone.

q: In Next.js server code, a teammate stores the current customer's cart in a module-level variable "to avoid fetching it twice per request". What is the main risk?
options: One module instance serves every request: customers see each other's carts
It is reset at the start of every request, so the cache never saves a fetch
Module-level variables are forbidden in server code, so the build fails
The variable is serialized into the HTML, so the cart leaks to the browser
explain: A module is evaluated once and shared by all importers for the life of the process, so module state on a server is shared across requests and users: a data leak between customers and a memory leak. Per-request data must live in the request scope; the "reset on every request" option describes what the teammate wrongly assumes.

q: A server-side cache of price labels grows without limit. It is a module-level Map keyed by product id, and products change rarely. Which fix would you ship?
options: Replace it with a WeakMap keyed by product id, so the GC frees entries
Clear the whole Map every hour with setInterval to cap its growth
Call the garbage collector at the end of each request to reclaim it
Bound it: an LRU with a maximum size, plus a time limit if prices change
explain: A bounded LRU keeps memory flat and keeps the useful entries; a Map's insertion order gives one in a few lines. A WeakMap cannot take a string id as a key (it throws "Invalid value used as weak map key", measured), and clearing everything hourly throws away the hot entries while still growing between clears.

q: A click handler on the storefront runs a 400 ms loop. When can the browser paint the result of the click?
options: Every 16 ms during the loop, because rendering runs on its own schedule
Only after the handler and the microtasks it queued have finished running
Right away, because painting happens on the GPU thread
Halfway through the loop, when the browser interrupts the task
explain: Rendering is a step of the event loop on the main thread, and it happens only between tasks, after the microtask queue is empty. Nothing interrupts a running task, so the screen stays frozen for the whole 400 ms. The refresh rate sets when a rendering opportunity may come, not whether a busy thread can be interrupted.

q: A developer from the Node team writes storefront code. Which statement about the browser event loop is true?
options: It has the same phases as libuv: timers, then poll for I/O, then check for setImmediate
process.nextTick callbacks run before promise callbacks, as in Node
setImmediate is the fastest way to yield to rendering
No nextTick or setImmediate; after a task and its microtasks, a frame may render
explain: Browsers have no libuv phases: one task runs, then all microtasks, then possibly a rendering step with rAF, style, layout and paint. Both process.nextTick and setImmediate are undefined in Chromium (checked). The nextTick-before-promises rule is specific to Node (M01).

q: What does this print in the browser?
explain: Synchronous code first (1, 5), then the microtasks in the order they were queued (3, then 4), then the timer task (2). Measured in Chromium, 10 runs out of 10. queueMicrotask and a .then callback share the same queue, so neither has priority over the other.

q: Code schedules setTimeout(f, 0) and requestAnimationFrame(g) in the same task. Which runs first?
options: f, always, because timers are tasks and frames come after tasks
g, always, because animation frame callbacks have the highest priority of all
Either one: it depends on when the next rendering opportunity falls
Both run in the same microtask checkpoint, in call order
explain: The timer is a task that is ready almost at once, while rAF waits for the next rendering opportunity, which follows the display refresh. Measured in Chromium over 200 random starts: the frame came first 134 times and the timer 66 times. Neither callback is a microtask.

q: What is a long task, and why does it hurt INP?
options: A fetch that takes more than 1 second; INP counts network time
A task over 50 ms; while it runs the browser cannot paint the next frame after an input
Any task over 16 ms, because it always drops a frame, and INP counts the frames that were dropped
A task that runs in a Web Worker for more than 200 ms
explain: web.dev defines a long task as any task over 50 ms. INP measures from an input to the next paint, and a long task on the main thread delays that paint and any input queued behind it. Network waiting does not occupy the main thread, and a worker's long task does not block the page.

q: Why does the storefront's yieldToMain() prefer scheduler.yield() over setTimeout(resolve, 0)?
options: Both let input and paint happen, but scheduler.yield() resumes before other queued tasks
scheduler.yield() runs the rest of the function on another thread
setTimeout cannot be awaited, so the function would not wait
scheduler.yield() is a microtask, so the function resumes sooner and the work finishes faster
explain: Both create a new task, so input and rendering can happen in between. The continuation of scheduler.yield() is prioritized: measured in Chromium, it resumed before a timer queued earlier, 20 runs out of 20, while a setTimeout continuation goes to the back of the queue. It is not a microtask (a microtask would block rendering) and not another thread.

q: The empty search panel loads "recent searches" and "trending products", both optional. With Promise.all, a trending failure empties the whole panel. What do you change?
options: Use Promise.race so the faster block is shown
Use Promise.any so the panel shows whichever of the two blocks succeeds first and skips the other
Wrap Promise.all in a retry loop until both succeed
Use Promise.allSettled, render each block from its own result, and report the failures
explain: allSettled never rejects and gives one result per input, so each optional block can fall back to empty on its own while the failure is reported. Promise.any would return only one of the two values, and race returns whichever settles first, even a failure. Retrying hides the outage and delays both blocks.

q: A search fetch was given { signal }, and the code calls controller.abort() while the response is pending. What does the fetch promise do?
options: It resolves with a response whose status is 499
It stays pending forever, so the caller must check signal.aborted
It rejects with a DOMException named AbortError
It rejects with a TypeError named NetworkError
explain: Measured in Chromium: the fetch rejected with a DOMException whose name is AbortError, and the test server saw the connection close. With AbortSignal.timeout the name is TimeoutError instead. 499 is a status some proxies log for a client that disconnected; the browser never makes up a response.

q: Why can the naive search handler show suggestions for "ru" after the customer typed "run"?
options: Responses can arrive out of order, and the handler renders whichever arrives last
The browser sends requests to the same host one at a time, in reverse order
fetch caches the first response of the session and returns it again for similar queries
React batches the state updates and keeps the first one
explain: Each keystroke starts a request, and the server may answer a short query more slowly than a longer one. Reproduced in Chromium with "ru" answered in 400 ms and "run" in 100 ms: the screen ended on "ru". Browsers send requests in parallel, and the bug happens in plain JavaScript without React.

q: Which description matches a trailing-edge debounce of 300 ms?
options: It runs at most once every 300 ms, for as long as the calls keep coming in
It runs once, 300 ms after the last call, with the arguments of that last call
It runs the first call at once and ignores the others forever
It runs every call, each delayed by 300 ms
explain: Every call restarts the 300 ms wait, so the function runs only after a pause, with the latest arguments; tested with fake timers, calls every 100 ms never triggered it until they stopped. "At most once every 300 ms while calls keep coming" is a throttle.

q: A function throttled at 200 ms (leading and trailing) is called every 50 ms for one second, then the calls stop. How many times does it run?
options: 20 times, once per call, since no two calls overlap
Once, 200 ms after the last call, with the arguments of that call
5 times, once at the end of each 200 ms window during the second
6 times: at 0 ms, then at the end of each 200 ms window
explain: The leading call runs at 0, and the latest call of each window runs when the window ends: tested with Vitest fake timers, it ran at 0, 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1,000 ms. Running once after the last call is what a debounce does.

q: What can code inside a Web Worker do?
options: Read and update the DOM of the page directly, but from a separate thread
Share JavaScript objects with the page by reference, so no copy is ever made
Call fetch and compute, and exchange copied messages with the page
Run only synchronous code, since it has no event loop
explain: A worker has its own thread and event loop, has fetch, and has no DOM (document is undefined inside one, checked in Chromium). Messages are copied with the structured clone algorithm; only transferable objects such as ArrayBuffer are moved instead, and even then nothing is shared by reference.

q: What does this print?
options: A B C E F D
A F B C E D
A B F C E D
A B F E C D
explain: loadCart runs synchronously up to its await, so B prints right after A. The rest of loadCart (C) was queued as a microtask before the .then callback (E), so C comes before E, and the timer (D) comes last. Measured in Chromium, 10 runs out of 10. A B C E F D forgets that await always suspends, even on a non-promise value.

q: A unit test triggers the "Add to cart" button with button.click(). The button has two click listeners, each queuing a promise callback. In what order do the logs appear?
options: listener 1, listener 2, after click(), micro 1, micro 2
listener 1, micro 1, listener 2, micro 2, after click()
after click(), listener 1, listener 2, micro 1, micro 2
listener 1, micro 1, listener 2, micro 2, then after click() in a later task
explain: click() dispatches the event synchronously, while the test code is still on the stack, so no microtask can run until that script ends. Measured in Chromium: listener 1, listener 2, after click(), micro 1, micro 2. The order with micro 1 between the listeners is what a real user click produces, because each listener then starts with an empty stack.

q: What does this print?
options: a1 a2 b1 b2
a1 b1 a2 b2
b1 b2 a1 a2
a1 b1, then a2 and b2 in the next task
explain: Only a1 and b1 are queued at first. Running a1 resolves the promise of the second .then, which queues a2 behind b1; then b1 queues b2. So the chains interleave: a1 b1 a2 b2, measured in Chromium. Everything happens in the same microtask checkpoint, with no task in between.

q: What is the order of the logs, as measured in Chromium?
options: frame, next frame, micro, timeout
frame, timeout, micro, next frame
frame, micro, next frame, timeout
frame, micro, timeout, next frame
explain: Microtasks are drained right after each rAF callback, so micro follows frame. A rAF requested inside a rAF callback waits for the next frame, about one refresh later, while the timer task is ready at once: measured 30 runs out of 30 in Chromium, headless and in a visible window. The nested rAF never runs in the same frame.

q: To fix the sticky search box, a colleague splits the filter into slices with await Promise.resolve() between them. Typing is still frozen. Why?
options: The slices are too large: with 100 entries per slice, the browser would find time to paint
Promise.resolve() is synchronous, so await does nothing at all
Code after await runs as a microtask, and all microtasks run before any paint or input
Chromium disables yielding inside input event handlers
explain: Awaiting a resolved promise does suspend the function, but it resumes in a microtask, and the microtask queue is drained completely before any rendering or next task. Measured in Chromium: 0 frames painted during 500 ms of work sliced this way. Smaller slices change nothing; a new task is needed, such as scheduler.yield() or setTimeout.

q: Profiling shows each keystroke spends about 300 ms in index.filter((entry) => normalizeForSearch(entry.label).includes(needle)) over 200,000 entries. What do you do first?
options: Normalize each label once when the index loads, and filter on the stored result
Move the same code to a Web Worker
Wrap the filter in useDeferredValue
Split it into slices with scheduler.yield() and keep normalizing each label per keystroke
explain: Most of the 300 ms is repeated work: normalizing 200,000 labels on every keystroke. Precomputing it brought one run to 26 ms in Chromium, at no architectural cost. Slices or a worker would still repeat the waste; they are the next steps if the remaining work is still too long.

q: What happens when the out-of-stock product is added?
options: The toast appears, because the error is thrown inside the try block of onAddClick
The page crashes and reloads
The toast appears after a microtask, when the rejection reaches the catch
No toast: the call returns a rejected promise, which goes unhandled
explain: An async function never throws at the call site; it returns a rejected promise. Without await, the try/catch has nothing to catch, and the rejection becomes an unhandledrejection event while the page keeps running (measured in Chromium). The fix is async onAddClick with await addToCart(productId).

q: A product page uses Promise.all([getReviews(), getStock(), getRecommendations()]). The stock call rejects after 10 ms; the others take 30 and 60 ms. What happens?
options: Promise.all waits for all three, then rejects with an AggregateError
It rejects after about 10 ms with the stock error; the other two calls still finish
It rejects after about 10 ms with the stock error and cancels the two other requests
Promise.all resolves with undefined in place of the stock result
explain: Promise.all rejects as soon as one input rejects, with that reason. It receives promises that are already running and cannot stop them: measured in Chromium, both slower calls settled after the rejection. Cancelling them needs an AbortSignal; AggregateError comes from Promise.any.

q: After a refactor, every fast typist sees "Search failed" banners. What is the bug?
options: With a reason, fetch rejects with that Error, so the name check misses it
abort() must be called after the new controller is created
An AbortError is a TypeError in browsers, so instanceof DOMException is false
The banner shows because aborting closes the connection with an HTTP error status
explain: When abort() receives a reason, fetch rejects with that reason: measured in Chromium, the rejection was the Error passed to abort. The name check therefore fails and a deliberate cancel is shown as a failure. Without a reason the rejection is indeed a DOMException named AbortError, so checking the signal (as section 6 does) is the robust test.

q: The response headers for "ru" have arrived and await response.json() is in progress when the next keystroke calls abort() on that request's controller. What happens?
options: Nothing: once fetch has resolved, the signal is no longer looked at
response.json() resolves, but with an empty object
The browser finishes reading the body and then throws on the next fetch
response.json() rejects with an AbortError, because abort also covers the body
explain: The signal stays attached to the response body. Measured in Chromium: aborting after fetch resolved but before the body was read made response.json() reject with an AbortError. Only once the body has been fully read does abort change nothing.

q: The suggestions now come from a Web Worker that answers with postMessage. Old answers sometimes overwrite new ones. Which fix would you ship?
options: Pass an AbortSignal to worker.postMessage
Tag each request with an increasing id and render only the latest id's answer
Terminate the worker and create a new one on every keystroke, so old work is dropped
Wrap the handler in Promise.race with a timeout
explain: A worker message cannot be aborted, so the fix is to ignore stale answers: measured in Chromium, 6 of 7 answers were dropped by the id check while typing. postMessage takes no signal, and recreating the worker would reload its index on every keystroke. Promise.race only picks the first to settle, not the latest query.

q: This handler is supposed to ignore stale responses. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing: the id check prevents the race
++latestId is not atomic, so two keystrokes can get the same id
The check runs before the await, where it is always true
The function must be synchronous for the id to be captured
explain: Right after the increment, requestId always equals latestId, so the check never skips anything. Staleness can only be detected after the await, when newer keystrokes may have raised latestId. JavaScript runs one callback at a time on the main thread, so the increment cannot be interleaved.

q: In this component, typing r, ru, run quickly sends three searches. Why?
options: Each render creates a new debounced function, so no calls are merged
setInput cancels the pending timer, so every value is sent right away instead
React StrictMode calls the handler twice
The debounce delay is too short for fast typists
explain: Every keystroke sets state, the component renders again and creates a fresh debounce; each instance receives one call and fires it 300 ms later. Measured in jsdom with React 19.3: r, ru, run were all sent, and with useMemo only run was. A longer delay changes nothing; debouncing the value with an effect avoids the problem.

q: With this module's debounce, a function is debounced with { leading: true, trailing: true } and called exactly once. How many times does it run?
options: Twice: once at once, once after the wait
Zero times, because the two edges cancel each other
Once, after the wait
Once, at the moment of the call
explain: The leading call runs at once and does not store its arguments, so at the end of the wait there is nothing left for the trailing edge. Tested with fake timers: a single call ran once, and a second call within the wait added one trailing run. Running twice would send a duplicate request for every single keystroke.

q: The results page loads the next page of products when the customer nears the end of the list. The current code runs a throttled scroll handler that measures the last card. What would you ship instead?
options: A debounced scroll handler, so it runs only when scrolling stops
An IntersectionObserver watching a sentinel element placed near the end of the list
A requestAnimationFrame loop that measures the last card on every frame
A setInterval that checks the scroll position every 100 ms
explain: Detecting that an element becomes visible is what IntersectionObserver is for; MDN lists infinite scrolling as a use case, and no code runs on the main thread during the scroll. A rAF loop or an interval would measure layout constantly, and a debounce would load late, only after the customer stops.

q: The first worker version receives the 200,000-entry suggestion index from the page with worker.postMessage(index) at startup. The page now has a 200 ms long task when it loads. Which change fixes it?
options: Let the worker fetch the index itself, so only small messages cross threads
Post the index from a microtask, so it does not block the page while it loads
Call postMessage inside requestAnimationFrame
JSON.stringify the index before posting it, because strings are not cloned
explain: postMessage copies the data with structured clone on the sending thread: measured in Chromium, posting the index blocked the main thread for about 200 ms. Fetching it inside the worker means the big data never crosses threads. A microtask or rAF only moves the same long task, and stringifying is still main-thread work.

q: A classic script in the head of the product page takes 800 ms to arrive. Which resource does the browser not start downloading during those 800 ms?
options: The product photo in an <img src> further down the HTML
A stylesheet referenced by a <link rel="stylesheet"> after the script
A background image declared in an inline <style> block
An async script referenced further down the HTML
explain: The preload scanner reads the markup and fetches what has a src or href, so the photo, the stylesheet and the async script start early (the photo was requested after 34 ms in the measurement). A CSS background is only known once styles are applied to an element, which happened after the script ran, at about 840 ms.

q: The head of a page holds a stylesheet that takes 800 ms and no script. What do you observe?
options: DOMContentLoaded fires early, and the first paint waits for the stylesheet
Both DOMContentLoaded and the first paint wait for the stylesheet
The page paints unstyled content first, then repaints when the stylesheet arrives
Neither waits: stylesheets never block anything in modern browsers
explain: Measured in Chromium: DOMContentLoaded at 24 ms, first paint at 872 ms. CSS blocks rendering, not parsing. DOMContentLoaded would wait only if a classic script followed the stylesheet, because that script waits for the CSS. Browsers do not paint unstyled content first on purpose: that is what render blocking prevents.

q: Two defer scripts are in the HTML: app.js (arrives after 600 ms), then product-page.js (arrives after 100 ms). When does product-page.js run?
options: At 100 ms, as soon as it arrives, even if app.js is still loading
Right after the parser reaches its tag, before the rest of the HTML is parsed
After DOMContentLoaded, in the order the files arrived from the server
After app.js, once parsing is done and before DOMContentLoaded
explain: Deferred scripts run after parsing, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded: measured, both ran at about 640 ms, app.js first. Running on arrival is the async behaviour. That is why one slow deferred script delays every deferred script after it.

q: The sticky add-to-cart bar slides in. Which property lets the browser animate it without running layout?
options: transform: translateY()
bottom, animated from -60px to 0
margin-top, animated with a transition
height, animated from 0 to 60px
explain: transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor without layout or paint; measured in Chromium, a transform change caused a style recalculation and no layout. bottom, margin-top and height are geometry: each change runs layout, and in an animation that happens on every frame.

q: A listener is on the grid, and the customer clicks the icon inside an Add to cart button. In the grid's listener, what are event.target and event.currentTarget?
options: Both are the button
target is the grid, currentTarget is the icon
target is the icon, currentTarget is the grid
target is the button, currentTarget is the document
explain: target is the element that was actually clicked, the deepest one, here the icon. currentTarget is the element whose listener is running, here the grid. That is why delegation uses target.closest('button') rather than assuming target is the button.

q: Why does a delegated listener on the grid also work for cards loaded after it was registered?
options: Because the browser copies listeners onto new children automatically
Because clicks on new cards bubble up to the grid's single listener
Because closest() registers a listener on each matching element
Because the capture phase starts at the grid rather than at window
explain: A click on any descendant bubbles through its ancestors, so the grid's listener runs whatever card was clicked, including one inserted later (measured). Browsers never copy listeners to new elements, and closest() only walks up the tree; it registers nothing.

q: What is a forced synchronous layout?
options: A layout the browser runs once per frame, just before paint
A layout triggered by a CSS animation running on the compositor thread instead of the main thread
A layout caused by a web font finishing to load and replacing the fallback font
A layout run immediately because a script reads geometry after a style change
explain: Reading offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect() after a style change forces the browser to compute layout right away, inside the script. The once-per-frame layout is the normal case. In the measurement, 500 interleaved reads and writes forced 500 layouts.

q: The server sets sid=…; HttpOnly and theme=dark. What does document.cookie return, and what does a fetch to the same site send?
options: Both cookies, and the fetch sends both of them
An empty string, and the fetch sends only theme
theme=dark, and the fetch sends only theme
theme=dark; the fetch sends both
explain: HttpOnly hides a cookie from JavaScript, not from the network: measured, document.cookie showed theme=dark while the fetch carried sid and theme. That is the point of HttpOnly for a session: the browser still authenticates requests, and an injected script cannot read the id.

q: Each file's arrival time is in the comment. In which order do the four scripts run?
code:
<script defer src="/a.js"></script>  <!-- 600 ms -->
<script async src="/b.js"></script>  <!-- 500 ms -->
<script async src="/c.js"></script>  <!-- 50 ms -->
<script type="module" src="/d.js"></script>  <!-- 50 ms -->
options: a, b, c, d
c, d, b, a
c, b, a, d
d, c, b, a
explain: Async scripts run on arrival: c at 50 ms, b at 500 ms. The module is deferred by default, so it waits for parsing and runs after a, keeping document order with defer scripts. Measured in Chromium with the same delays. "c, d, b, a" treats the module like async, which it is only with the async attribute.

q: What does this log when the button itself is clicked, in a current Chromium?
options: capture listener, then bubble listener
bubble listener, then capture listener
Only bubble listener
Only capture listener
explain: Measured in Chromium 156: at the target, capturing listeners run before non-capturing ones, whatever the registration order. Registration order would put the bubble listener first, which was the old behaviour at the target. Both always run, since neither stops propagation.

q: After a consent banner script was added, no Add to cart button reacts anymore, although their listeners are still registered. What is the most likely cause?
options: The banner set pointer-events: auto on the body
The banner added a bubble listener on the document that calls preventDefault()
The banner replaced EventTarget.prototype.addEventListener
The banner calls stopPropagation() in a capture listener on the document
explain: A capture listener on document runs before any listener deeper in the tree, and stopPropagation() there stops the event before it reaches the buttons (measured). preventDefault() cancels only the default action and does not stop other listeners, and a bubble listener on document runs after the buttons anyway.

q: This runs on every resize for 500 cards and took 540 to 640 ms in Chromium on a laptop. Which change would you ship first?
options: Wrap the loop in requestIdleCallback so it runs when the page is idle
Delete the script: the CSS grid row already stretches the cards
Read getBoundingClientRect() instead of offsetHeight, which is cheaper
Debounce the resize handler so the loop runs at most every 200 ms
explain: Each iteration writes then reads, forcing a layout per card. Grid items already stretch to the row height (measured: 252 px for both cards), so the script is not needed at all. getBoundingClientRect() also forces layout, and debouncing only makes the half-second freeze rarer.

q: The sticky bar must appear when the main Add to cart button leaves the screen. Which implementation would you ship?
options: An IntersectionObserver on the main button that toggles the bar
A scroll listener that reads getBoundingClientRect() on the button each time
A scroll listener, throttled to 100 ms, that reads the button's offsetTop
A setInterval every 50 ms that compares scrollY with the button position
explain: The observer calls back only when visibility changes (measured: 2 callbacks for 10 scroll events) and the page reads no geometry. The other three read layout on a schedule; throttling reduces the cost but still reads geometry on the main thread during scrolling.

q: A designer asks for the size selector to highlight with a new background-color. Which steps of the pipeline does the change run?
options: Style, layout, paint and composite
Only composite
Style, paint and composite
Only layout
explain: A colour changes pixels but not geometry, so layout is skipped: measured, a background change caused a style recalculation and no layout. Composite-only is reserved for transform and opacity, and layout never runs alone without style before it.

q: The storefront gets an access token after login. A colleague proposes storing it in IndexedDB "because it is not localStorage". What would you ship instead?
options: Keep IndexedDB, but encrypt the token with a key stored in the same database
Store it in sessionStorage, so it is deleted when the customer closes the tab
Store it in a non-HttpOnly cookie so both the server and the page can read it
Tokens stay on the server (BFF); the browser gets an HttpOnly session cookie
explain: OWASP notes that one XSS can read all of Web Storage and IndexedDB, and an encryption key stored in the same place is readable too. sessionStorage shortens the lifetime but is just as readable by an injected script. Only an HttpOnly cookie keeps the credential out of JavaScript entirely (M12).

q: What does this print?
options: { items: 2 } number
[object Object] string
It throws a TypeError on the first line
{"items":2} string
explain: Web Storage keeps strings only and converts values with String(), so the object becomes "[object Object]" and 3 becomes "3" (measured). Nothing throws, and nothing calls JSON.stringify for you: you must serialise and validate yourself.

q: Tab A updates localStorage.cartCount. Tabs A and B both listen to the storage event. Which tabs receive it?
options: Only tab B
Only tab A
Both tabs
Neither: the event is for sessionStorage only
explain: The storage event fires in the other documents of the same origin, not in the one that made the change (measured). That makes it a cheap way to sync a cart badge across tabs; the writing tab updates its own UI directly.

q: Which set of values makes a page "good" on all three Core Web Vitals, measured at the 75th percentile?
options: LCP under 4 s, INP under 500 ms, CLS under 0.25
LCP at most 2.5 s, INP at most 200 ms, CLS at most 0.1
LCP at most 1.8 s, INP at most 100 ms, CLS at most 0.05
LCP at most 2.5 s, INP at most 100 ms, CLS at most 0.25
explain: web.dev sets the good lines at 2.5 s for LCP, 200 ms for INP and 0.1 for CLS, at the 75th percentile of visits. The first option lists the "poor" lines: values between the two sets are "needs improvement", not good.

q: A product page answers its first tap at once, but the size filter used later takes 400 ms to repaint. Why did it pass FID and fail INP?
options: INP adds the time spent downloading the handler's JavaScript, which FID ignored
INP is measured by Lighthouse in the lab on a throttled phone, while FID came only from real users in the field
FID only counted key presses, so taps on the filter chips were never measured at all
FID timed only the wait before the first handler; INP times every interaction up to the next paint
explain: INP looks at all clicks, taps and key presses of the visit and measures from the input to the next painted frame, handler time included. FID only measured the wait before the first handler of the first interaction, so a slow later filter was invisible to it. INP cannot be measured in the lab at all, since it needs real interactions.

q: Lighthouse on a developer laptop gives the product page an LCP of 1.9 s, but Search Console lists the page group as Poor for LCP on mobile. What explains the difference?
options: Search Console reads CrUX: 28 days of real Chrome visits at p75, mostly phones; Lighthouse is one load
Search Console runs its own Lighthouse audits with a slower network profile and a throttled CPU, so its numbers are always higher
Search Console reports the mean of all visits, and a handful of very slow visits pull that mean far above the median
Lighthouse only measures text blocks for LCP, while Search Console also counts images
explain: The Core Web Vitals report reads CrUX field data: real Chrome users, a rolling 28-day window, the 75th percentile, split by device. A lab run is one load under fixed conditions and cannot represent the slower quarter of mobile visits. Search Console does not run Lighthouse, and it uses the 75th percentile, not a mean.

q: Why does a Lighthouse report show Total Blocking Time instead of INP?
options: INP needs 28 days of data before it can be computed, so a single lab run reports a placeholder metric instead
INP is a Chrome-only metric, and Lighthouse reports only metrics that every browser engine supports
A lab load has no real interactions; TBT, the blocking part of long tasks, is its proxy
TBT replaced INP as a Core Web Vital in 2025
explain: INP needs real clicks, taps or key presses, which a Lighthouse load does not have. TBT sums the part above 50 ms of each long task after the first paint, which predicts how blocked the main thread is; web.dev calls it a lab proxy, not a substitute. INP is still a Core Web Vital, and TBT never replaced it.

q: The hero image of the product page has loading="lazy". What happens to LCP?
options: Nothing changes: the browser ignores loading="lazy" on images that are already in the viewport
LCP improves, because the browser can download the hero in parallel with the render-blocking CSS
LCP is no longer measured on the page, since lazy-loaded images are excluded from the candidates
The request waits for layout, which adds load delay; measured, it started at about 550 ms instead of 20 ms
explain: A lazy image cannot be fetched by the preload scanner: the browser waits for layout to know whether it is near the viewport, even when it is in it. web.dev says never to lazy-load the LCP image. The first option is the common belief, but the decision needs layout, which waits for the stylesheet.

q: The storefront renders its hero with next/image and only src, alt, width and height. What does the Next.js 16 documentation say to change?
options: Nothing: next/image detects the largest image above the fold and raises its priority automatically
Add the priority prop, which Next.js 16 recommends for every image that might be the LCP element
It is lazy by default: set loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high", and add sizes
Replace it with a CSS background image, which the browser fetches together with the stylesheet
explain: The Image docs give lazy as the default loading and recommend loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high" for the LCP image in most cases; without sizes, the browser assumes 100vw. Next.js 16 deprecated priority in favour of preload. A CSS background is invisible to the preload scanner, which makes LCP later.

q: Why does web.dev prefer await scheduler.yield() to await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0)) for breaking up a long handler?
options: scheduler.yield() runs the rest of the function on another thread, so the main thread stays free for input
setTimeout does not let the browser paint between two tasks, while scheduler.yield() forces a frame first
Both end the task, but the scheduler.yield() continuation runs ahead of tasks of the same priority
scheduler.yield() works in every browser today, while setTimeout(0) is being deprecated for this use
explain: Both end the current task, so the browser can paint and handle input; measured, both kept a 300 ms handler's interaction at 16 ms or less when called before the work. The difference is the queue: scheduler.yield() continuations are prioritised, so other scripts do not slip in before the rest of your work. It is not in Safari, hence the setTimeout fallback.

q: A colleague "fixes" the size filter like this. Measured in Chromium, about how long does the tap interaction take?
options: About 300 ms: the code after await resumes in a microtask, before the browser can paint
Under 16 ms: the await ends the current task, so the frame is painted before the work
About 150 ms: the browser paints the pressed chip halfway through the filtering work
It depends on the network, because the promise resolves asynchronously after the next tick
explain: A resolved promise resumes the function in a microtask, and microtasks run before the browser leaves the task to render. Measured in Chromium: 304 to 312 ms with await Promise.resolve(), and the same with awaiting requestAnimationFrame, against 16 ms or less with scheduler.yield() or setTimeout. Async syntax does not end a task.

q: The LCP attribution of a product page reads: TTFB 300 ms, resource load delay 1,900 ms, resource load duration 400 ms, element render delay 100 ms. Which fix would you try first?
options: Make the hero discoverable: an <img> in the server HTML with fetchpriority="high"
Compress the hero image further and serve it as AVIF to make the download shorter
Move the HTML rendering to a faster server or region to cut the time to first byte
Reduce the JavaScript that runs after the image is downloaded, to shorten the render delay
explain: Load delay is 70% of the total, against a guideline under 10%: the browser starts the request late, typically because the image is lazy, a CSS background or inserted by JavaScript. Compression shortens the load duration, which is already reasonable; work on the biggest part first.

q: Another product page has a TTFB of 2.1 s at p75 and a well-optimised hero image. Which fix addresses the biggest part of its LCP?
options: Add fetchpriority="high" to the hero image so the browser requests it before anything else
Preload the brand font so the text is painted earlier
Serve the page from a CDN cache and remove redirects in front of it
Split the JavaScript bundle with dynamic imports so the page needs less code to start
explain: Nothing starts before the first byte of HTML, and 2.1 s is above web.dev's poor line for TTFB (1.8 s). Caching the page at the edge and avoiding redirects attack that part directly. Image priority and code splitting act after the first byte, so they cannot recover time spent waiting for the server.

q: The team ships the LCP fix on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Search Console still shows the product pages as Poor. What do you tell the product manager?
options: The fix failed: Search Console recomputes the report every night from the previous day's visits
Google must re-crawl the pages first, so request indexing for each product URL in Search Console
The report only updates after someone runs Lighthouse on the page in PageSpeed Insights
CrUX covers 28 days, so it moves slowly; check RUM p75 for the new release now
explain: Group metrics in the report come from 28 days of CrUX data, so one day of better visits barely moves the p75, and a validation runs a 28-day monitoring session. Your own RUM split by release shows the effect within hours. Requesting indexing does not change field data, which comes from real visits.

q: On mobile, 80% of product page visits have an LCP of 2.5 s or less, and the other 20% are between 3 and 6 s. What is the page's LCP status?
options: Good: the 75th percentile is at most 2.5 s
Poor: some visits are above 4 s
Needs improvement: the average is above 2.5 s
Poor: more than 10% of visits are above the good line
explain: The status uses the 75th percentile: if 80% of visits are at or under 2.5 s, the p75 is too, so the page is good. The slowest quarter does not count, which is why p75 tolerates a long tail; neither the average nor the share of poor visits is used.

q: The back office has a p75 INP of 120 ms. A manager asks you to spend two weeks rewriting its orders table to raise its Lighthouse score from 70 to 95. What is the senior answer?
options: Accept: a higher Lighthouse score improves the app's ranking in Google Search results
Accept, but first move the table rendering to a web worker so the score rises faster
Refuse any performance work on internal tools, since Core Web Vitals only matter for SEO
Push back: field INP is already good and the app is not indexed; invest where agents feel slowness
explain: Field p75 says the interactions agents feel are already good, and an internal app has no search ranking to gain. The senior move is to ask what users feel and invest there, not to chase a lab score. Refusing all performance work goes too far: INP on internal tools still costs agents time when it is poor.

q: The filter handler now shows the selection and yields, then runs 300 ms of work in one block. A user taps a second size 100 ms after the first. Measured in Chromium, what happens to the second tap, and what fixes it?
options: Nothing: the first yield already ended the interaction, so all later taps are fast too
It waits about 200 ms; slicing the work with yields brought it to about 20 ms
It cancels the first filter, because the browser aborts the running task when new input arrives
It is dropped: the browser discards input that arrives during a long task
explain: The yield helps the first tap paint, but the 300 ms block that follows is still one long task, and the second tap waits for it as input delay: measured about 200 ms. With 20 ms slices and yields, the second tap got its turn within a slice: 16 to 24 ms. Browsers never discard or abort input or tasks this way.

q: An interviewer asks: "Our site feels slow. Where would you start?" Which answer shows the senior approach?
options: Ask for field p75 by page type and device, take the worst metric, and split it into parts
Run Lighthouse on the home page and fix every audit it lists, starting with the highest weight
Upgrade to the latest framework version, which ships the newest performance optimisations
Add memoisation to every component to cut re-renders
explain: Field data says where users suffer and which metric is poor; splitting it (LCP parts, INP phases) says which fix will move it. Fixing every Lighthouse audit spends time on items with no field impact, and blanket memoisation or upgrades are solutions looking for a problem.

q: The back office renders <p>{review.body}</p>, and the body is <img src=x onerror="steal()">. What does React 19 produce?
options: An <img> element whose onerror runs when the image fails to load
A render error, because React refuses text that contains HTML
The payload as text inside the paragraph, with < encoded
An <img> element whose onerror attribute React removed before insertion
explain: A value between braces is text: react-dom/server encoded it as <img … onerror="…, and react-dom/client inserted a text node (measured with 19.3.1). React does not strip attributes from user HTML because it never parses it as HTML in the first place; that would be a sanitiser's job.

q: A customer saves a review containing a script payload, and it runs later in the browser of every agent who opens the order. Which kind of XSS is it?
options: Stored XSS
Reflected XSS
DOM-based XSS only
Clickjacking
explain: The payload is saved on the server and served to other users later: that is stored XSS. Reflected XSS travels in the request (a URL parameter) and comes back in the immediate response. The sink here happens to be in the front end, but what defines the kind is where the payload lives.

q: React 19.3 renders <a href="javascript:alert(1)">site</a>. What is in the DOM?
options: The same href; React only logs a warning in development builds
An anchor with no href attribute at all
Nothing: rendering throws and the component does not mount
An href React swaps for a javascript: URL that throws an error
explain: React 19 swaps the URL for javascript:throw new Error('React has blocked a javascript: URL as a security precaution.'), in both the development and production builds of react-dom 19.3.1 (measured on the server and in Chromium, where clicking the link threw instead of running the code). Nothing is removed, and rendering does not fail.

q: Which of these is not covered by React's automatic encoding?
options: A string rendered as a child: {review.body}
The __html value of dangerouslySetInnerHTML
A string in a title attribute
A string in a data-review-id attribute on the card
explain: dangerouslySetInnerHTML is the explicit escape hatch: its string is inserted as HTML, as is (measured: the <img onerror> came out intact). Text children and attribute values are encoded, which is why the other three are safe.

q: Product insists that reviews keep bold, italics and lists. Which technique makes rendering that HTML safe?
options: Sanitisation with an allow-list, right before the HTML sink
Validation with a regular expression at the API boundary, before saving
Output encoding of the whole review before rendering
A Content Security Policy instead of any change to the code
explain: Only a sanitiser keeps the allowed formatting while removing everything else. Encoding the whole review would display the tags as text, which defeats the requirement, and validation cannot decide what is safe HTML in every context. CSP is a second layer, not the fix.

q: Why does the team sanitise reviews in the component that renders them, rather than only once before saving?
options: Because DOMPurify cannot run in Node, so the API could not call it before saving
Because storing sanitised HTML breaks database indexes
Because safety depends on the final string at the sink, and later edits can undo it
Because sanitising twice would double-encode the text
explain: The DOMPurify README warns that modifying HTML after sanitising can void it, and the allow-list may change after the data was stored. Sanitising at the sink checks the exact string that reaches the browser. DOMPurify does run in Node, given a jsdom window.

q: An XSS runs on the storefront. Compare a refresh token in localStorage with a session held behind an HttpOnly cookie by a BFF.
options: The token can be copied and replayed elsewhere; the cookie cannot be read
Both are equally exposed: an injected script can read the cookie and the token alike
Both are safe: same-origin policy keeps scripts away from both
The cookie is worse, because fetch sends it to any site the script calls
explain: Web storage is readable by any script of the origin, so the token leaves with the attacker. HttpOnly forbids reading the cookie, but the browser still attaches it to requests from the infected page, so XSS prevention still comes first. And fetch attaches a cookie only to requests for the host that set it, not to any site the script calls.

q: What does CORS control?
options: Whether the server accepts and runs a request coming from another origin
Whether the browser attaches cookies to a request
Whether the caller is authorised to perform the action
Whether a script from another origin may read the response
explain: CORS relaxes the same-origin policy on reading. In every measurement of section 7, the server received and ran the request whatever the Origin. Cookie attachment is SameSite's job, and authorisation is the server's.

q: A Vite app's .env contains VITE_PAYMENT_SECRET=sk_live_oops, used in client code. What does vite build do with it?
options: It refuses to build because the value looks like a secret
It inlines the value as plain text in the JavaScript bundle
It encrypts the value with a per-build key that only the page can read
It exposes the value only in the development server
explain: Measured with Vite 8.3.4: the bundle contained 'sk_live_oops' as a string literal, while an unprefixed variable became void 0. Vite's docs say VITE_* variables should not contain sensitive information such as API keys.

q: A server-rendered search page embeds the query for hydration. The URL is ?q=</script><script>steal()</script>. What happens in the browser?
options: The query closes the script element early and the attacker's script runs
JSON.stringify escapes the angle brackets, so the query stays a harmless string
React encodes the __html of a script element, so nothing runs
The browser parses the JSON first, so the query stays a string
explain: The HTML parser ends a script element at the first </script>, before any JavaScript is parsed, and JSON.stringify does not escape <. Measured in Chromium: the injected script ran and window.__SEARCH__ was never set. Replacing < with \u003c fixed it.

q: Reviews have an optional "unboxing video" URL rendered as <a href={videoUrl}>. Which fix would you ship?
options: Wrap it in encodeURIComponent(videoUrl) before passing it to href
Nothing: React 19 already blocks dangerous URLs
Parse it with URL and allow only https: and http:
Remove the substring javascript: with a replace
explain: Parsing and allow-listing the protocol rejects javascript: with any casing, spacing or tab, and data: URLs too (measured on Node 24). React blocks only javascript:, so data: passes; encodeURIComponent breaks valid URLs; and a substring replace misses java\tscript:.

q: A colleague proposes to sanitise review HTML with html.replace(/<script[\s\S]*?<\/script>/gi, ''). Why do you reject it?
options: Regular expressions are too slow for 5,000-character reviews
Payloads need no script tag: onerror handlers and javascript: URLs pass a deny-list
It is unnecessary, because browsers never run any HTML that is inserted with innerHTML
Regular expressions cannot match Unicode characters
explain: Scripts inserted with innerHTML do not run, which is precisely why attackers use <img onerror> and similar. A deny-list must predict every vector; an allow-list sanitiser such as DOMPurify keeps only known-safe elements and attributes. The third option is half true and dangerous: other HTML inserted that way does run handlers.

q: An agent logs in; the BFF sets a cookie with no SameSite attribute. Thirty seconds later, the agent opens a page on evil.example that auto-submits a form POST to the back office. What does Chromium do?
options: Sends it: Lax by default still allows a top-level POST for 2 minutes
Withholds it: without the attribute, Chromium applies SameSite=Strict to every request
Sends the cookie: without the attribute, Chromium applies None
Rejects the cookie at login because it has no SameSite attribute
explain: Measured: the cookie was sent on the cross-site POST right after login, and not sent after 125 seconds, when plain Lax applied. A Lax default with that 2-minute exception is why you set SameSite explicitly. Chromium treats the missing attribute as Lax, not None.

q: An XSS runs on www.shop.example. It calls fetch('https://backoffice.shop.example/api/me', { credentials: 'include' }), and the back office cookie is SameSite=Strict. Is the cookie sent?
options: No: Strict blocks every cross-origin request
No: HttpOnly cookies are never sent by fetch
Yes: both hosts are the same site, so SameSite does not apply
Only if the back office answers the preflight with CORS headers allowing it
explain: SameSite compares sites (shop.example), not origins. Measured: the Strict cookie was attached, and the server received it even when it sent no CORS headers; CORS only decided whether the script could read the answer. That is why the BFF rejects Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site on state changes.

q: In code review you find this BFF setting, and the session cookie is SameSite=None; Secure. What is the impact?
options: None: SameSite=None still blocks cross-site requests
Any site the agent visits can read the agent's API responses
Nothing: browsers refuse to honour a reflected origin when credentials are included
Only preflighted requests are affected
explain: Measured: a script on evil.example fetched /api/me with credentials and read the JSON, cookie included. Reflecting Origin with credentials allows every origin to read; use an exact allow-list, or no CORS at all for a same-origin SPA. SameSite=None is precisely the setting that allows cross-site sending.

q: An API answers Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. A script on another origin calls it with credentials: 'include'. What happens?
options: It works: the cookies are sent and the response is readable
The browser strips the cookies and lets the script read the response
The server receives nothing: the browser cancels the request
The browser hides the response: * is not allowed with credentials
explain: Measured in Chromium: fetch rejected with "Failed to fetch" and the console said the header "must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'". The request itself still reached the server (measured); only the reading was blocked, so this misconfiguration fails safe but breaks the feature.

q: The BFF's cookie is SameSite=None. Which request from evil.example reaches POST /orders/ord_a1/refund with the cookie, without a preflight?
options: fetch(url, { method: 'POST', mode: 'no-cors', credentials: 'include', body: '{"amountCents":999}' })
fetch(url, { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' } })
fetch(url, { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: { 'x-requested-by': 'backoffice' } })
fetch(url, { method: 'PUT', credentials: 'include', body: '{"amountCents":999}' })
explain: A no-cors POST with a string body is sent as text/plain, a "simple" request, so no preflight (measured: the server saw the POST with the cookie). JSON, custom headers and PUT trigger an OPTIONS preflight, and since the BFF approved nothing, the real request never left. That is why the BFF requires application/json.

q: With the isAllowedStateChange guard of section 7, what does this call return?
options: true, because same-site requests come from one of the shop's own subdomains
true, because a JSON body cannot be forged cross-site
false: only same-origin passes when Sec-Fetch-Site is present
It throws, because the origin is not in the allow-list
explain: The guard accepts a state change only when Sec-Fetch-Site is same-origin, and falls back to the Origin list only when the header is missing (run on Node 24: false). Accepting same-site would let an XSS on the storefront issue refunds through the back office.

q: In the storefront, a Client Component calls a helper that reads process.env.SEARCH_ADMIN_KEY (no prefix). The helper does not import server-only. What happens in the browser?
options: The admin key is inlined in the client bundle as a plain string literal
The build fails with an environment error
Next.js fetches the value from the server at runtime
The reference is replaced with an empty string, so the call fails
explain: The Next.js docs: only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are included in the client bundle, and others are replaced with an empty string. Nothing leaks, but the bug is silent; importing server-only in the helper turns it into a build-time error.

q: The checkout has <div class="btn" onclick="pay()">Pay now</div> next to a real <button>. What did Chromium do with the div?
options: It exposed it as a button, because a click handler is attached to it
Tab skipped it and the accessibility tree showed it as plain text
Tab reached it, but neither Enter nor Space triggered its click handler
It exposed it as a link, because the pointer cursor changes on hover
explain: A click handler adds no role and no focusability: Tab went straight to the next control and the tree listed "text: Pay now". "Tab reached it but keys did nothing" describes a div with role="button" and tabindex="0", which still lacks the keyboard behaviour of a real button.

q: What is the accessible name of <button aria-label="Close">Remove item</button>?
options: "Remove item", because the visible text always wins over attributes
"Remove item Close", because both sources are joined together
"Close", because aria-label comes before the content
No name at all, because the two sources conflict with each other
explain: In the accessible name computation, aria-label comes before naming from content, so Chromium named the button "Close". That is exactly why it is a bug: the visible label is no longer in the name (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name), so a voice control user saying "click Remove item" fails.

q: In the back office SPA, the agent presses Enter on the "Order 42" link. The router removes the old page, link included, and renders the new one. Where is keyboard focus, measured in Chromium?
options: On body, because the focused element was removed
On the new page's h1, moved by the browser
On the first focusable element of the new page
Still on the removed link, which keeps focus while detached
explain: When the focused element leaves the DOM, document.activeElement falls back to body and a screen reader announces nothing. The browser never moves focus to the new heading on its own: that is the job of code such as the PageHeading component, which focuses an h1 with tabindex="-1".

q: A button is styled with button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid }. Which interaction showed the outline in Chromium?
options: A mouse click on the button
Any focus, whatever the input device
Only a programmatic button.focus() after a mouse click
Reaching the button with Tab or Shift+Tab
explain: Measured: keyboard focus matched :focus-visible, while a mouse click on the same button focused it without matching. Browsers use heuristics so that keyboard users always see focus and mouse users clicking a button do not, which is why styling :focus-visible beats deleting the outline.

q: With @layer base, components;, base contains #checkout button { color: red } and components contains .pay-button { color: green }. What colour is the Pay button?
options: Red, because an id selector is more specific than a class selector
Red, because base is declared first and keeps priority
It depends on which of the two rules comes last in the file
Green: a later layer wins whatever the specificity
explain: Layers are compared before specificity: the later layer, components, wins. Measured in Chromium, the button was green. Specificity only decides between declarations of the same layer, which is what makes layers useful against legacy id selectors.

q: Code review on the storefront. Which change do you ask for?
options: Add role="button" and tabIndex={0} to the div so keyboards reach it
Add aria-label="Pay" so that screen readers can announce a name
Replace the div with <button type="button">
Add an onKeyDown handler that calls onPay when Enter is pressed
explain: A native button brings the role, focusability, Enter and Space activation, the disabled state and form behaviour. Role and tabindex alone left Enter and Space doing nothing in Chromium, and an Enter handler still misses Space; aria-label would only name a control that keyboard users cannot reach.

q: What name does Chromium compute for the button?
code: Delivery address
options: "Delivery address"
"Edit address"
"Edit"
"Edit address Delivery address"
explain: aria-labelledby comes first in the accessible name computation and overrides both aria-label and the content: measured, button "Delivery address". The tempting "Edit address" would be right only without aria-labelledby.

q: A voice control user says "click Remove item" on a cart line and nothing happens, while a mouse click works. The markup is <button aria-label="Close">Remove item</button>. What is the cause?
options: Voice control only activates links, so the button must become a link
The name is "Close", so the spoken label matches nothing
The button needs tabindex="0" before voice control can reach it
Voice control reads the title attribute, and this button has none
explain: aria-label replaced the visible text in the name, and voice control matches what the user can see. WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name requires the visible text to be part of the name. A button is already focusable, so tabindex changes nothing here.

q: The back office is a React SPA. Which fix would you ship so that screen reader users notice a page change?
options: Put aria-live="assertive" on main so the new page is read out
Call document.body.focus() after each navigation to reset focus
Give the h1 of every page tabindex="0" so Tab reaches it
Update the title and focus the new h1 (tabindex="-1")
explain: Focusing the heading makes the screen reader read it and makes the next Tab start there (measured). tabindex="-1" allows focus() without adding the heading to the Tab order, whereas tabindex="0" would add a useless Tab stop on every page. An assertive live region around main turns every content update into an interruption, which MDN advises against.

q: What colour is the Pay button, measured in Chromium?
options: rgb(0, 0, 255), because unlayered styles always beat layered ones
rgb(1, 1, 1): important reverses the layer order
rgb(2, 2, 2), because components is the later of the two layers
rgb(0, 0, 255), because it is the last declaration in the file
explain: For !important declarations the order is reversed: earlier layers beat later ones, and layered important beats unlayered important. Measured: rgb(1, 1, 1). "Unlayered beats layers" is true only for normal declarations, which is the trap here.

q: Which rule colours the Pay button?
options: Green, because four classes add up to more than one id
Green, because it comes later in the file
Both apply and the browser blends them
Red, because one id outweighs any number of classes
explain: Specificity is compared column by column: (1,1,0) against (0,4,0), and the id column decides before classes are counted. Measured in Chromium: red. Source order only matters when specificity is equal.

q: The Filters menu has z-index: 9999 but opens under the sticky header (z-index: 10). Its toolbar has transform: translateZ(0). Which fix works?
options: Raise the menu to z-index: 99999 so it beats the header
Add position: relative to the menu so z-index applies
Make the menu a popover (top layer)
Add isolation: isolate to the toolbar to reset stacking
explain: The transform makes the toolbar a stacking context, so the menu's z-index only competes inside it. A popover is drawn in the top layer, above the header (measured). Any child z-index fails, and isolation: isolate creates the same kind of context, so the menu stayed under the header in that test too.

q: A developer adds container-type: inline-size to an inline-block wrapper around a product card, and the card disappears. Why?
options: Container queries only work on elements inside a grid layout
